iCal in Mac OS X Lion, 2011

Apple’s desktop calendar in Lion, with a stitched tan leather top bar and torn paper edges, the most cited example of the style’s excess.

Source
Apple, “Mac OS X Lion: New features” (archived July 2011)
Creator
Apple
Made
2011 (Mac OS X Lion); renamed Calendar in OS X Mountain Lion (2012); leather removed in OS X Mavericks (2013)
Style
Skeuomorphism (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Tactile, ornate, warm
Evidence
Apple’s archived Lion features page describes the “streamlined new look” of iCal; its screenshot of the app is only 323 × 199 px, too small to describe. The leather design is documented by Fast Company (2012) and by the style record’s sources.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Apple’s Lion page said iCal “features a streamlined new look that gives you more room to browse and edit your events.” Apple, archived July 2011.

A former senior Apple UI designer told Fast Company that “iCal’s leather-stitching was literally based on a texture in his Gulfstream jet,” meaning Steve Jobs’s jet. Fast Company, Austin Carr, “Will Apple’s Tacky Software-Design Philosophy Cause A Revolt?” (2012).

Wikipedia’s lead on skeuomorphs uses “a software calendar that imitates the appearance of binding on a paper desk calendar” as its virtual example, citing Wired (2012). Wikipedia: Skeuomorph.

Why it belongs

The leather is decoration from a luxury interior, not from a calendar. That is why critics used it as the clearest sign of the style going too far.

What to review next
